records.name: Clearview Ranch Solar and Battery Project
records.description: Clearview Ranch Solar and Battery Project is a data center approved but not yet built in Macon County, AL, developed by Alabama Power. The project represents 200 MW of planned capacity. It was first announced in 2026. The project spans Macon and Bullock counties; the county field records Macon only because the schema carries a single county string. Alabama Power submitted project information to Commission Staff and the Attorney General on July 2, 2026. Alabama Daily News reports a target commercial operation date of June 30, 2029, roughly 485,000 MWh of first-year production, a 35-year expected solar life and 20-year battery life, and about $110 million in state and local tax impact over two decades ($56 million Bullock, $27 million Macon). Environmental permits and other federal and state reviews remain outstanding before construction can begin. Recent developments — Aug. 4, 2026: At its August 4, 2026 meeting the Alabama Public Service Commission approved the Clearview Ranch Project under Docket 32382, Case No. 2026-1, together with the accompanying Renewable Subscription Program contract between Alabama Power and Dotier, LLC.

records.description: Alabama Supercomputer Center is a data center operating in Huntsville, Madison County, AL, developed by Alabama Supercomputer Authority. The building spans nearly 24,000 square feet and houses the authority's Security Operations Center, Network Operations Center, Data Recovery Center, data center and operations offices. Power and cooling capacity are not published. Single-source record: the operator's own facility page. records.description: Atlas Development Stiles Road Data Center (Euharlee Road) is a data center stopped or paused in Cartersville, Bartow County, GA, developed by Atlas Development LLC. The site plan showed seven structures of about 260,000 sq ft each. The Etowah River lies to the west; county Community Development Director Brandon Johnson said the site is directly across the river from Georgia Power's Plant Bowen and that a power easement runs through the property. No capacity or investment figure was disclosed, and no Georgia DRI filing was found for the project. Recent developments — November 2025: Atlas Development applied for a conditional use permit for a data center on about 302 acres at 208 and 329 Stiles Road, off Euharlee Road; a Bartow County Planning Commission hearing was set for 2025-12-15 (reported 2025-11-14 from the county's legal advertisement). records.name: Project Red Clay
records.regulatory_body: Lowndes County Commission; Lowndes County Economic Development Commission
records.description: Project Red Clay is a proposed hyperscale data center campus from Houston- and Seattle-based Cloverleaf Infrastructure on more than 800 acres of farmland in northeast Lowndes County, near the junction of U.S. 80 and Alabama 21 at Burkville, about six miles southwest of Montgomery and along the Selma-to-Montgomery National Historic Trail. Cloverleaf, a speculative developer that assembles powered land for an operator it has not named, has requested 1,500 MW from Alabama Power and describes the project as at least a $1.5 billion investment with more than 1,000 construction workers and 225 to more than 300 permanent jobs at full scale. The county has no planning or zoning authority, so the decision ran through the Lowndes County Commission, which on Oct. 13, 2026 voted 3-2 at a 10-minute regular meeting to approve the project development agreement and a 20-year, 50 percent abatement of non-educational property taxes and construction and equipment sales taxes; the agenda had listed only a resolution to schedule a later special meeting. Estimates of the abatement’s value range from about $1.15 billion (Alabama Reflector) to $2.4 billion (Southern Environmental Law Center); Cloverleaf projects $2.85 billion in local tax revenue over 20 years and pledged $10 million through the Central Alabama Community Foundation. Two residents who live near the site, Marie Barnes and Felicia Williams, sued the commission under the Alabama Open Meetings Act on Oct. 18. The presiding judge recused himself and retired Circuit Judge Collins Pettaway Jr. was appointed; he denied an emergency restraining order on Oct. 21, and when the first hearing opened Oct. 27 he continued it to Dec. 2 at 1:30 p.m. to give the plaintiffs time to find a property-value expert. The commission approved the Oct. 13 minutes 3-2 on Oct. 20 as about 125 residents protested. Cloverleaf says construction will begin in early 2027, and the end user has still not been disclosed.

records.name: Edged Prichard Data Center (Project Gateway)
records.regulatory_body: Prichard City Council; Prichard Planning Commission
records.description: Project Gateway is Edged Energy’s planned data center in Prichard, north of Mobile, the first large data center proposed in the Mobile area. The project ran into a dispute after the city issued a building permit on July 30, 2026, days before the council adopted a six-month data center moratorium; the city then questioned whether the permit was valid because the required site-plan review had not happened, and Edged’s attorney threatened litigation in September. On Sept. 29 the Prichard Planning Commission approved the site plan after the city acknowledged the permit had been issued out of order, clearing the project to proceed outside the moratorium. Edged attorney Doug Anderson said construction would begin soon and take about 18 months. Mayor Carletta Davis’ fiscal 2027 budget counts on revenue from the project, and Edged has said its design uses waterless cooling.

records.name: Nebius Birmingham AI Factory (BHM01)
records.regulatory_body: Birmingham City Council; Zoning Board of Adjustment; Oxmoor Steering Committee
records.description: Nebius, the Amsterdam-based AI cloud company, is building its first U.S. AI factory, BHM01, on a wooded site in Birmingham’s Oxmoor Valley. The campus is planned for about 300 MW in its first phase on roughly 470 acres, and Nebius has said it could invest more than $1 billion. Construction is running six days a week, 12 hours a day. The project has drawn four lawsuits: a suit by the Sansome couple whose home abuts the site, an Oxmoor Valley homeowners’ class action, a challenge by the Greater Birmingham Humane Society over its neighboring campus, and a fourth separate action. Three of the cases have been partially consolidated. The litigation has focused on how the land changed hands — the site sold three times in a single day, for $17.2 million and then $83.5 million — and in October 2026 plaintiffs sought records and testimony from Iron City Premier Realty, the brokerage founded by Mayor Randall Woodfin’s wife Kendra Woodfin; the city and her attorney objected. Defendants agreed on Oct. 7 to turn over closing documents and on Oct. 20 moved to dismiss the homeowners’ suit. Birmingham’s data center moratorium has since expired and been replaced by an ordinance that sorts facilities into micro, medium and hyperscale tiers and requires hyperscale operators to use closed-loop cooling.

records.name: Oakley Real Estate Partners Brown Farm Road Data Center
records.description: Oakley Real Estate Partners Brown Farm Road Data Center is a data center stopped or paused in Cartersville, Bartow County, GA, developed by Oakley Real Estate Partners. Approvals run through the Bartow County Board of Commissioners. Rezoning request by Akin & Tate P.C. on behalf of Oakley Real Estate Partners for about 111.4 acres at the west end of Brown Farm Road, near the Etowah River, from A-1 (agricultural) to Business Park District, with a land-use-map change from low density residential to industrial. Oakley described it as a micro-scale data center it intends to market; no end user has been named. The plan is two buildings of about 374,000 sq ft in total, with a power substation and a single access drive, and a voluntary condition that the campus never exceed 450,000 sq ft. Other self-imposed conditions: setbacks of at least 200 ft from residential areas, and no cryptocurrency mining. Oakley estimated about 50 jobs and roughly $5 million a year in property taxes. At the Planning Commission hearing, Oakley said the substation and the nearest building would each sit 400 ft from the riverbank. The hearing was first set for 2026-07-27 but was removed from that agenda after county staff found a discrepancy in the notice sent to Native American nations with ties to the district. The Planning Commission voted 6-0 to recommend denial on 2026-08-24; the commissioner's 2026-09-02 agenda listed zoning applications, but as of 2026-09-30 neither the meeting minutes nor any press report of the final decision had been found. No Georgia DRI filing exists for the project. No capacity or investment figure has been disclosed. Oakley Real Estate Partners had proposed a micro-scale campus capped at 450,000 sq ft on 111.4 acres in the Etowah Valley Historic District. Recent developments — July 2026: Akin & Tate P.C., on behalf of Oakley Real Estate Partners, applied to rezone about 111.4 acres off Brown Farm Road from A-1 to Business Park District and to change the land use map from low density residential to industrial; Oakley presented the plan at a 2026-07-15 community meeting. On 2026-08-24 the Bartow County Planning Commission voted 6-0 against both requests, sending recommendations for denial to the sole commissioner for a final decision at his 2026-09-02 meeting.

records.name: Project Camellia (OpenAI Effingham County Campus)
records.regulatory_body: Effingham County Industrial Development Authority; Board of Commissioners; Georgia PSC
records.description: Project Camellia is OpenAI’s planned hyperscale campus inside the Savannah Gateway Industrial Hub near Rincon, in Effingham County, announced in July 2026 and described as a roughly $20 billion investment. Filings show four data center buildings totaling about 4.4 million square feet on a 1,400-acre site, with Georgia Power contracted to deliver 3.2 GW between 2028 and 2032; OpenAI says it will pay the full cost of the electric infrastructure and can shed up to 1 GW of load during peak periods. The company has pledged an $80 million community fund, from which it announced the first $2 million for Atlas Park, a recreation area on a former sand mine, plus up to $71 million in Codex credits for Georgia college students. The Effingham County Industrial Development Authority approved a payment-in-lieu-of-taxes agreement on Aug. 31 after negotiating the deal under a nondisclosure agreement, which has become the central grievance of residents and the Protect Effingham Alliance. Two lawsuits are pending: three residents sued the county on Sept. 2 to void Ordinance 2026-352, which added data centers to industrial zoning, alleging required hearings were skipped; and on Sept. 21 the Southern Environmental Law Center and One Hundred Miles sued the IDA, which had listed the item on its agenda only as “Project Gateway,” and on Oct. 27 asked Judge Michael Muldrew to void the land-sale agreements without a trial. On Oct. 5 OpenAI’s affiliate Octans GA applied to the Army Corps of Engineers for a Clean Water Act permit to fill 72 acres of forested wetlands (application SAS-2026-00872); the company says its layout preserves 70 percent of the site’s wetlands and adds stormwater controls. Public comment closes Nov. 4, and One Hundred Miles is pressing for a public hearing. The state released the full Development of Regional Impact report on Oct. 14, and the county hired Charles Abbott Associates on Oct. 20 to oversee Phase 1 reviews.

records.name: QTS Bessemer (Project Marvel)
records.regulatory_body: Bessemer City Council; Bessemer Planning Commission
records.description: Project Marvel is a QTS Data Centers hyperscale campus taking shape on roughly 1,600 acres in southwest Bessemer near Rock Mountain Lake, the largest single private investment ever proposed in Alabama at about $14 billion. The plan calls for 18 buildings of roughly 250,000 square feet each, more than 4 million square feet in all, with a planned power draw of about 1.2 GW from Alabama Power and closed-loop cooling that would use up to 130,000 gallons of municipal water a day. The land was assembled by Atlanta-based TPA Group’s Logistic Land Investment LLC and sold to a Blackstone-affiliated buyer in deals worth more than $870 million; QTS, which is owned by Blackstone, confirmed in July 2026 that it is the developer. Bessemer added data centers to its industrial zoning in October 2025, rezoned the original parcel 5-2 that November and rezoned 914 additional acres in April 2026, widening buffers. Neighbors sued in April 2026 over notice and endangered-species concerns. The project became the defining issue of the 2026 city election: Mayor Kenneth Gulley, who had signed a nondisclosure agreement with the developer, lost his runoff in September to Louise Alexander. On Oct. 19 Mayor Alexander sent QTS a cease letter asking it to halt clearing, grading and blasting until the city reviewed the project’s permits; QTS responded that site development is proceeding under permits the city already issued, declined to pause, and postponed a planned Oct. 23 meeting. Homeowners outside the city limits have been approached by a broker working for QTS, with at least one given a Dec. 18 deadline, and Jefferson County is weighing a 1,000-foot buffer for homes in unincorporated areas. QTS told ABC 33/40 on Oct. 27 that it is taking no local, county or state incentives or abatements, projects more than $1 billion in tax revenue over 20 years, expects about 5,000 construction jobs at peak and 330 to 350 permanent jobs, and plans a five-to-seven-year phased buildout. It has committed $8 million to a Bessemer Built scholarship program and says it wants a community benefits agreement with the mayor.

records.name: Project Bunkhouse (Digital Realty Data Center Campus)
records.regulatory_body: Bartow County Board of Commissioners; Georgia DCA
records.description: Project Bunkhouse (Digital Realty Data Center Campus) is a data center proposed in Stilesboro, Bartow County, GA, developed by Digital Realty. The project represents a planned investment of $19 billion and 1300 MW of planned capacity. Approvals run through the Bartow County Board of Commissioners; Georgia DCA. Applicant of record is Taurus DC SPE LLC (Bartow County rezoning case Z-25-00020); no source reviewed names a parent company for that entity. Operator: Bartow County's August 2026 policy statement refers to the campus as "Digital Realty's investment in the Stilesboro area". The county's minutes of the June 4, 2025 hearing, summarizing the presentation by the applicant's attorney, Scott Peters, record: "This is a Digital Realty project. It is not a Crypto center.", and Andrew Alves of Digital Realty appeared as part of the Project Bunkhouse team at the May 19, 2025 planning commission hearing (Daily Tribune). Digital Realty has not announced the project in its own press releases. Taff Road south of GA Hwy 113, south of Georgia Power's Plant Bowen, also bordering Floyd Creek Church Road; tax parcels 0032-1184-001, 0032-1122-001, 0032a-003-002 and 0032b-003-006; Raccoon Creek runs along the property. the DRI filing states 8,675,000 sq ft; the approved rezoning caps total building area at 8,300,000 sq ft. Earlier, a site plan obtained by the Atlanta Journal-Constitution (April 2025) put the project's power needs at 1,830 MW with three on-site substations; the DRI filing's energy-demand field is blank. The same county statement says Bartow County has granted no tax abatements, PILOT or comparable arrangement to these data center facilities. Value: the DRI filing states an estimated build-out value of $19 billion and projected annual property tax of at least $40-50 million, with build-out estimated for 2035. Incentives: the DRI filing said the project was "in the process of incentive negotiations" with the Bartow-Cartersville Joint Development Authority; the county's economic development director, Melinda Lemmon, said that was "mistakenly included in the DRI filing" and that the authority "is not negotiating incentives with the data center calling themselves Project Bunkhouse or any other data center" (Daily Tribune, April 2, 2025). No bond validation, PILOT or abatement for the project has been found. Rezoning conditions include: an 8,300,000 sq ft cap; buffers required before occupancy; primary access from Taff Road only; distribution, manufacturing, warehousing, outdoor storage, towers, laboratories and retail prohibited; water-efficient HVAC required. No building permits or site work have been reported since the rezoning. DRI describes an 8.6M sq ft campus on ~860 acres on Taff Road near Plant Bowen, ~$19B, completion by 2035; needs rezoning to Business Park District. A hearing was set for May 19 (2025); outcome not found. Recent developments — Mar. 31, 2025: Bartow County submitted Development of Regional Impact #4433 ("Project Bunkhouse") to the Georgia DCA; determined to warrant regional review 2025-04-01. June 4, 2025: Sole Commissioner Steve Taylor approved rezoning case Z-25-00020 (applicant Taurus DC SPE LLC), 876.57 acres from A-1 to Business Park Development and the land-use map from Agricultural to Industrial, with conditions.

records.description: In Trinity, a small town in Morgan County west of Decatur, landowner John Eyster is asking the Town Council to rezone 184.12 acres between Steed Road and Old Trinity Road from agricultural to light and heavy industrial. records.name: Statewide: Alabama PSC data center contract rules (Act 2026-610 / Alabama Power tariff)
records.regulatory_body: Alabama Public Service Commission; Alabama Power
records.description: Alabama’s Act 2026-610 took effect Oct. 1, 2026 and requires the Public Service Commission to find that Alabama Power’s contracts with data centers of 150 MW or more cover their own costs and benefit other customers. The PSC approved its review framework 3-0 on Oct. 6 and issued its final order the week of Oct. 20, and Alabama Power filed the implementing tariff, which takes effect Nov. 23. Under the rules, unredacted contracts go to the PSC and the Attorney General’s office for review and a redacted version listing the location, maximum capacity and company must be made public, but contracts are deemed approved if the commission does not act within the review window and the cost figures behind each approval remain confidential. Alabama Power says large data center customers will pay the full cost of serving them.

records.description: On Oct. 22, 2026 Judge John T.
